uncited: Rendering Order and Strategy defines the sequence in which volumetric cells are processed during ray-grid traversal to ensure correct optical compositing (typically front-to-back) and efficient occlusion culling.

It solves the problem of determining which cells contribute to the final pixel color and in what order, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by decoupling the geometric traversal logic (handled by the parent [Ray-grid traversal](17-ray-grid-traversal.md)) from the semantic processing order required for correct alpha blending or visibility determination.
The family shares the fundamental requirement that cell processing must respect the viewing direction to correctly accumulate opacity and color.

While the parent [Ray-grid traversal](17-ray-grid-traversal.md) provides the geometric sequence of voxel indices visited by a ray, the rendering strategy determines how these visits are mapped to the final image buffer.

The core principle is that for standard volume rendering with absorption, processing must occur from the camera towards the volume interior (front-to-back) to allow early termination when the ray becomes fully opaque.

Strategies may also involve spatial partitioning (e.g., layers, octants) to group cells for batch processing or to handle complex hierarchical data structures where implicit occlusion rules replace per-ray depth sorting.
The distinction between object-order (volume-driven) and image-order (pixel-driven) rendering strategies has been fundamental since the early days of volume visualization.

Image-order methods, like backward projection, became standard for ensuring consistent pixel coverage and simplifying the compositing logic, particularly as hardware acceleration for ray-box intersection and texture sampling improved.

The development of hierarchical strategies like Front-to-Back Layer Traversal addresses the specific needs of complex, nested data structures where traditional linear traversal is inefficient for occlusion culling.
